query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The favorable strength–ductility balance of the Co‐free FeNiCrMn HEA derives from a grain‐boundary–mediated dislocation nucleation mechanism: GBs (especially high‐energy or specific misorientation boundaries) serve as preferential sites for the nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ partial dislocations, which rapidly generate stacking faults that interact with and impede further dislocation motion. This self‐adjusting process delays catastrophic yielding and maintains ductility. Its dynamic signature (e.g., lower nucleation stresses and earlier onset of stacking fault formation relative to single crystals) is modulated by temperature and strain rate.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified, equiatomic, single-phase FCC Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Prepare samples with controlled GB character (e.g., bicrystals with well-defined high-energy (e.g., Σ111 with small twist angle) versus low-energy/coherent (e.g., Σ3) GBs) and conduct uniaxial tensile tests over a range of temperatures (room temperature to ~1000 K) and strain rates (10^7 to 10^9 s⁻¹)
generation.conditions: Tests carried out under controlled temperature and strain rate regimes where previous ballistic impact simulations and tensile tests (e.g. PMC9374344) indicate similar mechanisms, with the comparison made between samples with prominent GB networks versus essentially GB-free (single crystal) microstructures
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary structure which facilitates the nucleation of specific partial dislocation lines leading to stacking fault formation
generation.mechanism: Upon loading, GBs act as heterogeneous sites for the nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ partial dislocations that propagate into the bulk, leaving behind stacking faults. These faults interact with further dislocation motion to enhance strain hardening and delay failure. At higher temperatures, increased dislocation mobility softens the material yet the GB-assisted nucleation remains operative, preserving ductility despite lower peak stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to single-crystal HEA samples, bicrystals with high-energy GBs will show: (a) an earlier onset (lower strain) of dislocation nucleation and stacking fault formation, (b) a more pronounced drop in peak stress at nucleation, and (c) relatively preserved ductility through enhanced strain hardening, even as elevated temperatures lower the absolute stress levels.
generation.baseline: Single-crystal Co-free FeNiCrMn HEA exhibiting homogeneous nucleation of dislocations at higher strains and without the enhanced stacking fault density provided by GB mechanisms
generation.boundary: The mechanistic hypothesis applies within the FCC, solid-solution regime of the HEA and under deformation conditions (temperatures from ~300 K to 1000 K and strain rates in the 10^7 to 10^9 s⁻¹ range) where GB-mediated mechanisms have been identified in similar systems
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of GBs in facilitating dislocation nucleation and stacking fault formation is supported by evidence in related HEAs, the exact quantitative effect of temperature and strain rate on the nucleation stress levels and stacking fault densities in the Co-free alloy remains to be precisely determined. Additionally, local chemical variations at the GBs may modulate this mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Using specimens of the Co‐free FeNiCrMn HEA fabricated as both single crystals and bicrystals with well-defined GB characters (e.g., Σ111 vs Σ3), perform in situ tensile tests under identical temperature (e.g., 300 K and 1000 K) and strain rate (e.g., 10^8 s⁻¹) conditions. Monitor the evolution of dislocation nucleation and stacking fault formation using high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM with straining stage) or advanced diffraction techniques.
measurements: Stress–strain response (peak stress and ductility metrics)
Comparison of nucleation stress in bicrystals vs single crystals
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens with high-energy GBs do not exhibit a statistically significant lower strain threshold for dislocation nucleation and stacking fault formation, or if the stress–strain curves of bicrystals are indistinguishable from those of single crystals under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis that GB-mediated dislocation nucleation is responsible for the favorable strength–ductility balance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We conducted comprehensive microcompression tests on (CoNi)50(TiZrHf )50 with different crystal orientations and at varying temperatures to investigate the underlying deformation mechanisms. Utilizing the ion milling method, we fabricated micropillars measuring 1 μm in diameter and 2 μm in height (see Methods). As observed in Fig. 2a, the nominal stress–strain curves obtained from the micropillars with [100], [110], and [111] orientations are serrated and exhibit similar elastic stiffness and yield strength at RT, demonstrating weak elastic modulus and yield strength dependence on crystal orientation, a characteristic that considerably deviates from conventional crystalline alloys (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 3). This can be attributed to severe lattice distortion found in our HEIA, which mitigates the atomic bonding difference along various crystal orientations, therefore imparting isotropic-like behavior to our alloy. The nominal stress–strain curves from the [111] oriented micropillars at different temperatures clearly show that our B2 alloy’s serrated plastic flow at low temperatures becomes smooth with increasing temperature (Fig. 2c). Here, the PTM algorithm was used to identify the local structural environment around each atom and reveal GB regions and stacking faults that form during deformation. Figure 5 depicts results for the bicrystal system with a Σ9 [110] STGB, where Fig. 5a is a schematic illustrating the intersection of a {111} plane with this GB. Figure 5b–d shows respectively projected views normal to this {111} plane at nominal tensile strains ϵ=5.0%,5.4% and 5.5%, where the GB region is labeled in blue, FCC atoms in green, and HCP ones, indicative of stacking faults, in red. A 1/6 ⟨112⟩ partial dislocation line, identified by DXA and labeled in black, was observed to nucleate from the GB and propagate into the bulk crystal leaving behind a stacking fault, and that the nucleation of this partial dislocation corresponded to the stress drop observed for this bicrystal system (refer to Fig. 4b). Following the experimental approach by Laplanche et al., we quantified the microstructural evolution during mechanical deformation by calculating the fraction of stacking fault atoms with respect to the total in each system, and the results are reported in Fig. 8 for bicrystals with a [110] (Fig. 8a) and [111] (Fig. 8b) loading axis. Stacking fault atoms were identified as ones with HCP ordering using the PTM algorithm. As mentioned above, the observed stress drop in the stress–strain diagrams corresponded to the nucleation of partial dislocations from GBs, which in turn grew rapidly into the bulk crystals leaving behind faulted regions. No stacking faults were observed to nucleate prior to reaching the peak point in the stress–strain diagram. In all bicrystal systems, the rapid increase in the fraction of faulted atoms at lower strain values compared to the single crystal systems indicates that GBs serve as efficient nucleation sites for partial dislocations. Owing to the small twist angle, θ=9.43∘, of Σ111 and the well defined interfacial dislocation structure, this GB was found to be the most efficient in nucleating partial dislocations, i.e., it exhibited the smallest ultimate stress and strain values out of all [111] systems. On the other hand, dislocations were observed to nucleate homogeneously form the bulk crystals in the system with the coherent Σ3. For the bicrystal systems with a [110] loading axis, our results suggest that ultimate stress and strain values are lower for small (≲30∘) and large (≳60∘) twist angles compared to intermediate ones. The results depicted in Fig. 9 show that while each set of [110] and [111] bicrystal systems have the same maximum Schmid factors for slip and twinning, variations do exist due to the GBs present in these systems. The Schmid factor provides crystallographic directions with the most resolved shear stresses; however, as depicted in Fig. 9 our work shows that the presence of GBs plays a role in the dislocation nucleation process in HEAs.

While the Cantor alloy has been the subject of numerous studies in recent years, most of these have been mainly focused on the effects of element compositions away from the equiatomic one, stacking fault energies,, and lattice distortions. The role of GBs in the mechanical deformation of HEA alloys remains poorly understood. Tensile stress-strain diagrams for Cantor alloy bicrystals with [110] and [111] loading axes show that GBs facilitate the nucleation of partial dislocations, which with further deformation grow in the bulk crystal leaving behind stacking faults. This is in agreement with recent experimental findings demonstrating that GBs act as nucleation sites for mechanical nanotwins,. The bicrystals with a [111] loading axis were found to require more mechanical energy to nucleate dislocations from GBs compared to systems with a [110] loading axis. As shown in Figs. 5 and 6, nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ dislocations in the bicrystal systems occurred at lower strain values compared to their single crystal counterparts.
